item.title: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates
item.description: Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra.
item.dc:creator: Cisco Talos
item.content:encoded:
Cisco Talos is aware of eight intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority, eMudhra. Rather than possessing the mandatory 384 bits of pseudo-random security, several private keys evaluated single-digit and double-digit integers. This misconfiguration allows an attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs to impersonate any website or service. Six of the TLS certificates, trusted by Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have been blocked by these vendors already. Two other certificates, used for codesigning by Microsoft, have also been blocked. Talos expects there will be additional patches available across a variety of technologies as software applications work to remediate the certificates’ exposure.

Following the disclosure, eMudhra has revoked the compromised certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root.

Compromise details

The cause of this issue, originated during an April 30, 2025 key generation activity conducted by eMudhra under its emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and cross-signed Comodo AAA Certificate Services.  During a key generation ceremony for 24 subordinate CAs, a flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process created a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step. Those keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw took the encryption from 384 bytes of entropy down to 3 – 8, making recovering the private keys trivial. The following are the impacted certificates, as illustrated in Mozilla’s bug report:

EM EV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012304
SHA-256 E7568FE6E12331F4FD7DE61DA4C7559D0F8EB192A218D4741A3BA75184333838
serial c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3

EM OV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012308
SHA-256 98B896625C0C230ADEEC3EB2CF6AAD5001ECF9156A68644E82374CE5833BC25B
serial 6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3

EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012302
SHA-256 42C4ACCD12C4F59597925E1A08A7A90102608543809308D50EC427E118BA1493
serial a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3

EM EV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012296
SHA-256 432EC25F0D28DE9006D97BF752F17BBB2CD41F669933FCB072D9A1148D0261F3
serial 8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3

EM OV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012300
SHA-256 CB6E15165AC802E9B3F993F16C25D41F4E81C21EBDE71AE1B012AC00BF9C7C3F
serial 296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3

EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012294
SHA-256 0164D7CEAE5BB909C272AF151FF44B1177AE9B47D9424B94F1D9558C30934D19
serial 588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321, issuer emSign Root TLS CA - G3

EM OV CS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV), CCADB A012306
SHA-256 9E39DE2881273ACC225A149C72BA3E0F51424963669AB633EE1DC7DF5DB067B4
serial 7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a, issuer emSign Root CS CA - G3

EM OV CS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc), CCADB A012298
SHA-256 4B2460A466F95FD40113BCDCCA2CEB29B3B093921DE45474DA7DF48874C630B1
serial 544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6, issuer emSign Root CS CA - G3

CVE-2026-111943 

Unlike languages that defer entirely to external dynamic system libraries (like OpenSSL), the Go programming runtime implements its own X.509 chain verification engine in the standard library (crypto/x509). While Go usually queries platform certificates, several platforms or static container environments rely on embedded or legacy root certificate pools where certificate revocations are ignored. 

To eliminate exploitation across the entire cloud-native ecosystem including Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform, and Prometheus, the Go team designated the compromised certificates as a vulnerability, CVE-2026-111943, and released Go versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. 

 The fixed versions filter out chains containingthe SHA-256 hashes of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) for all eight compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates.

Impact

These compromised certificates could allow adversaries to impersonate servers and intercept or modify traffic. The impact of their exposure is far more than just web browsers. Other programs that check for TLS certificates might still be impacted since they may not check revocation lists. One clear example is related to virtual private networks (VPNs); these technologies will likely require software updates to mitigate the issue. Based on this guidance, Talos strongly recommends users update software using and handling TLS certificates as fixes become available.

Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these compromised certificates and has not seen any malicious incidents involving them in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC / 10:00 a.m. ET).

Significance of this breach  

Public key infrastructure relies on trust being delegated through certificate chains: root CAs authorize intermediate CAs, which can issue certificates within the scope of their authority. An attacker who obtains an intermediate CA’s private key may be able to issue fraudulent certificates that clients accept, subject to the intermediate certificate’s constraints and each client’s validation controls. In this incident, six compromised intermediates were for TLS and two were for code signing.

 For TLS, an attacker able to intercept or redirect a connection could use a fraudulent certificate to impersonate a server and potentially read or modify traffic if the client still trusts the affected key and no applicable protection blocks it. Protections such as revocation, key distrust, certificate transparency enforcement, and certificate pinning can prevent or expose such an attack. Browser vendors have blocked the affected TLS keys, but other applications may rely on separate trust stores or validation paths:

Enterprise infrastructure and VPNs

Organizations should assess TLS-using software and appliances, including proxies, reverse load balancers, VPN clients, and gateways. Exposure depends on the certificate chain being validated and the trust store and revocation behavior in use. A stale or separately managed trust store may need an application, operating-system, firmware, or trust-bundle update; verify the required action for each product.

Software supply chains and CI/CD

Build runners and package managers may be exposed if they fetch content over TLS while still trusting an affected key and an attacker can intercept the connection. A fraudulent TLS certificate could enable registry impersonation, but it would not by itself bypass separate package integrity checks, such as lockfile hashes, checksums, signatures, or provenance controls. Assess the actual package-manager configuration and dependency path.

Industrial IoT and embedded systems

Review devices that use bundled or independently managed CA stores, especially where certificate revocation or trust-store updates may be limited. Some devices may require a vendor update or compensating control, but the necessary action depends on each device’s validation and update mechanisms.

Talos recommends updating affected software and trust stores as vendor fixes become available.

Coverage

The following SNORT® SIDs provide coverage for this threat: 67363 - 67374.

 

Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Chris Morrison for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for this threat.

item.title: Two critical RCEs in PHP core
item.description: Two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP core could have implications across its wider ecosystem. Talos has published a blog to explain what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available, including rules in the Community Ruleset.
item.dc:creator: Cisco Talos
item.content:encoded:
Cisco Talos is tracking the disclosure of two unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) flaws in PHP core, dubbed “php2shell”, triggered by a plain HTTP request and exploitable before any application code runs, affecting every PHP build since 5.4. Based on the entities involved in the disclosure, artificial intelligence and associated technologies played a key role in the discovery of these vulnerabilities — yet another example of how these technologies are forcing change across the landscape, most notably on patching processes for organizations because of the wave of vulnerabilities being disclosed. 

Cisco customers are covered with the Cisco Talos Network Intrusion Prevention (SNORT®) signatures 67359 and 67360. These rules are also available in the Community Ruleset for open-source customers. Please refer to the following recommendations, detection, and coverage guidance for more information.

Details

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both critical vulnerabilities with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

  • CVE-2026-109618 occurs when out-of-memory handling interrupts PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat invalid data as valid.
  • CVE-2026-109619 occurs when a stale internal state is reused after its backing memory has already been freed, before normal initialization resets it.

Impact

The potential blast radius is enormous and extends across the PHP ecosystem. The vulnerability sits in PHP core, so applications running affected versions — including WordPress, Drupal, Magento, Shopware, WooCommerce, and Laravel, plus PHP sites hosted through cPanel or Plesk — may be exposed. Note that many older branches will no longer receive fixes, so customers are urged to upgrade to a supported version as soon as possible.

Talos regularly investigates threat actor exploitation of vulnerabilities. State-sponsored and affiliated threat actors, as well as ransomware and other financially motivated groups, all employ tactics to exploit RCE. Talos assesses that all industries running PHP applications are at risk for exploitation if systems remain unpatched.

PHP 8.1 and older are end of life (EOL), and PHP 8.2 security support ends Dec. 31, 2026. Talos’ initial estimates based on open-source intelligence show a significant corpus of PHP systems that will not receive a patch (~50%). If your organization is running PHP 8.1 or older, Talos very strongly advises immediate update to PHP 8.2 or later. There is no patch for PHP 8.1 or older.

Talos is actively monitoring the impact of these CVEs and has not seen them being exploited in the wild yet (as of October 21, 2026 14:00 UTC/10:00 a.m. ET).

Recommendations and detection guidance

Talos strongly recommends all PHP users to upgrade to the available fixed releases. There are no intermediate or temporary controls that provide comprehensive protection; however, PHP advises that the following measure may reduce exposure to specific attack paths:

CVE-2026-109618

  • Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.
  • Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Consider enforcing limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count, and nesting depth. These limits must also cover requests without a usable Content-Length.
  • Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause the vulnerable allocation failure.

CVE-2026-109619

  • Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.
  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.
  • Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not help.
  • Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts, including failures in callbacks, upload or import processing, and cleanup.

This is another vulnerability that owes its origin to AI and its associated technologies. As we move through 2026, the wave of vulnerabilities and related patches is building. Talos advises organizations to work on a triaged process for prioritizing vulnerabilities with a specific focus on public-facing systems and vulnerabilities that are under active exploitation. The glaring need to prioritize vulnerabilities along with a streamlined process for rolling out patching strongly indicates that the historic trend of “baking in” patches before deployment is not going to survive the AI era.

The true impact of this vulnerability will take time to evaluate. These types of vulnerabilities that impact core technologies tend to cascade into other platforms and applications as they evaluate impact and provide associated patching, harkening back to the waves of exploitation that we saw after Log4J.

Coverage

SNORT® SIDs covering these vulnerabilities for subscribers: 67359, 67360, 67375. Free community rules are live through our Community Ruleset.

Talos would like to highlight the efforts of Ankur Tyagi, Dalton Schaadt, Brandon Stultz, and Matt Killion for providing emergency coverage and mitigations for these threats.

item.title: Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers
item.description: Adversaries are turning the tools businesses trust into delivery mechanisms for malicious activity. Cisco Talos observed abuse of more than 25 legitimate platforms over the past year, exploiting the built-in trust of collaboration, file-sharing, payment and other services to reach their targets.
item.dc:creator: Diana Brown
item.content:encoded:
• Legitimate infrastructure has become a powerful delivery mechanism for attackers, carrying the inherent trust they once had to build. As Cisco Talos explored in our previous research on weaponizing software-as-a-service (SaaS) notification pipelines, these platforms are increasingly repurposed as proxies for malicious intent.  
  • Talos has since tracked a significant acceleration in this trend, observing abuse across more than 25 distinct legitimate platforms in the past year.  
  • The abused infrastructure included collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms.  
  • This demonstrates that attackers are not limiting themselves to traditional phishing infrastructure or lookalike domains. Instead, they are systematically subverting the very tools businesses trust.  

Order notification abuse 

Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines. Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos. 

The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number. 

In the first campaign, the message appeared as a Staples order confirmation from "support@orders.staples.com” with the subject line, “Here’s your Staples order #9939818875. Thanks for shopping with us.” The body displayed a plausible purchase for an Apple iPad, including order number, delivery timing, pricing, billing information and standard Staples footer content. The suspicious element was embedded in the order details: “Helpline 806 283 7712,” “Order Confirmed,” and the Staples corporate address appeared in fields normally associated with shipping or billing information. 

The structure of the message matters. The attacker was not trying to persuade the user to click a crude phishing link. Instead, the message created the impression that an expensive order had already been placed and that the fastest way to resolve it was to call the embedded “helpline.” The desired user action was a phone call. Once the victim moved from email to voice, the attacker could continue the scam through social engineering, payment manipulation, credential theft, or remote assistance fraud. 

The headers reinforced the trust problem. The Staples message showed DKIM alignment for “orders.staples.com” and DMARC passed for the visible Staples domain. The message also passed through forwarding and re-encapsulation paths, including Proton Mail, Microsoft 365, and downstream enterprise mail infrastructure. These hops complicate provenance analysis, but they do not change the core issue: Authentication helped establish that the outer message was credible, while offering no assurance that the phone number or transaction context was legitimate.  

The second campaign used the same pattern in a Dell order received notification. The message was sent from “Dell | Order Received <received@order.dellcom>” with the subject line, “We have your order | Dell Purchase ID: 2009829958247.” The body presented a purchase for Microsoft Project Standard 2024, totaling $736.09. As with the Staples example, the suspicious content appeared in transaction fields. The “Ship To” and “Bill To” sections included “Confirmed Order,” “Helpline 808 232 6397,” and “Call Our Sales Team”. 

The Dell message used the same psychological lever: an unexpected high-value purchase, a legitimate-looking order template, and a phone number positioned as the path to resolution. The attacker did not need the recipient to trust a new domain or unfamiliar brand. The message borrowed credibility from Dell’s order pipeline and redirected the recipient toward attacker-controlled contact information. 

Authentication results showed DKIM passing for Dell-related infrastructure and DMARC passing for “order.dell.com”. As with the Staples sample, forwarding artifacts and SRS-style return paths appeared as the message moved through Microsoft and enterprise mail infrastructure. But the malicious intent did not live in an obviously forged sender. It lived inside the rendered order content. 

These campaigns illustrate the same trust-boundary failure described in our earlier research on platform-as-a-proxy (PaaP) abuse. In those cases, attackers placed malicious content into SaaS fields that trusted platforms later rendered into notifications. Here, the same concept appears in commerce infrastructure, in the retailer’s order pipeline. The attacker supplies the intent, while the trusted system performs the delivery.  

From a defensive perspective, sender authentication is necessary, but it is not sufficient. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC help answer whether a message came from expected infrastructure. However, they do not answer whether the transaction was legitimate, whether the rendered fields make business sense, or whether the user is being pushed toward an attacker-controlled action. 

Order notifications should be treated as sensitive content. Any field reflected into a transactional message — shipping name, billing name, address line, company name, order note, support field, or fulfillment instruction — can become a delivery vehicle if it is not validated before rendering. Retailers and security teams should correlate order notification content with account history, payment state, shipping context, and known support channels. Transactional templates should reject or flag unexpected phone numbers, URLs, urgency language, and support instructions when they appear in fields where they do not belong. 

In both campaigns, the wrapper was legitimate enough to inherit trust. The payload was attacker-influenced. That distinction is the center of this attack class. 

The abuse of commerce pipelines is merely one manifestation of a broader, systemic vulnerability. Whether the attacker initiates a fake purchase or a fraudulent account sign-up, the root cause remains the same: Platforms are implicitly trusting data that enters their systems from untrusted sources, only to render that data into high-reputation, automated notifications. This same mechanism of reflection — where input is echoed back into an email to a third party — is the engine behind an evolution in list bombing, moving the attack from simple denial-of-service to a sophisticated vehicle for content delivery.  

List bombing: From inbox disruption to content delivery 

List bombing is an abuse technique in which attackers submit a victim’s email address to numerous legitimate registration, subscription or notification workflows, flooding the inbox with automated messages. While this vector is traditionally viewed as a denial-of-service or distraction tactic designed to bury critical alerts in a flood of junk, Talos has observed a subset of cases where this behavior is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle for malicious content. This abuse occurs when an attacker identifies public-facing registration, profile, or project-naming forms that lack sufficient input validation. By inputting a "hostile string" — such as a cryptocurrency-themed lure — into fields intended for a name, company, or title, the attacker forces the platform to treat this data as legitimate user information. When the service reflexively incorporates this input into its automated welcome, verification, or notification templates, the system acts as an unintended carrier, delivering the attacker’s content inside a high-reputation, system-generated email that can pass standard authentication checks. 

The attacker’s objective in these cases is to bypass the security perimeter by laundering their malicious content through the brand reputation of a trusted service provider. While this is not yet a broad industry shift, it represents a calculated abuse of a platform's trust boundary. By embedding their lure in an automated notification, the adversary ensures that the message arrives with the appearance of administrative legitimacy, significantly increasing the likelihood that the recipient will trust the content. The goal is to reach the target's inbox with enough platform authority that the message may be evaluated as routine notification traffic rather than attacker-controlled content. 

Beyond the risk to the individual recipient, this vector creates a significant brand liability. When a service provider’s infrastructure is used to broadcast fraudulent content, the resulting user complaints and bounce-backs can degrade the platform's own sender reputation, potentially triggering blocklisting that impacts their legitimate business communications. 

Bounce abuse: When delivery reports carry the lure 

The final vector moves the abuse pattern into the mail system itself. Instead of relying on a retailer, SaaS platform, or registration workflow to generate the message, the attacker attempts to make a delivery status workflow carry attacker-controlled content. 

Bounces, formally known as delivery status notifications (DSNs) or non-delivery reports (NDRs), are generated when a message cannot be delivered. Under normal conditions, a mail system sends the delivery report back to the original SMTP envelope sender. Depending on the implementation, that report may include the original headers, portions of the message body, URLs, attachments, or an encapsulated copy of the failed message. That returned content creates the abuse opportunity.  

In one example Talos observed, a mail delivery system notification carried a WeTransfer-themed file-sharing lure. The administrative wrapper made the message look like routine mail-system noise, while the nested content asked the recipient to engage with what appeared to be a file transfer workflow. The attacker’s goal was to make the phishing lure feel less like an unsolicited external message and more like part of a technical delivery failure that required review. Users are conditioned to view system errors as benign and are far more likely to engage with an "administrative" fix than a suspicious, standalone phishing email.  

There are several ways this kind of message can reach a victim. In opportunistic backscatter, an attacker sends mail using the victim’s address as the forged envelope sender. If an intermediate system accepts the message and later fails to deliver it, the resulting DSN may be sent back to the forged sender. If the DSN includes enough of the original message, the bounce itself can carry the lure. 

 A second possibility is intentional bounce abuse, where the attacker uses an authenticated, compromised, or otherwise controllable sending context to trigger a delivery failure that returns attacker-influenced content. This differs from an outright forged NDR, where the attacker simply fabricates the bounce message and sends it directly. From the recipient’s mailbox, however, these cases can look similar: A delivery-failure wrapper contains content the attacker wants the user to trust. 

This distinction matters for defenders. A DSN’s administrative appearance does not validate the content inside it. The outer message may be a legitimate delivery report, while the returned or encapsulated content may still contain a phishing link, credential harvesting page, malicious attachment, or social engineering prompt. 

The content-trust gap: A defensive imperative 

Across these vectors, the defensive failure is consistent: Trusted infrastructure is being treated as a shortcut for trusted content. 

Sender authentication remains essential. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, reputation, and infrastructure analysis help determine whether a message came from an expected source. But these controls do not answer a separate and increasingly important question: What was that trusted system instructed to carry? 

Order notifications, registration workflows and delivery reports all create opportunities for attacker-influenced content to appear inside messages that users and security tools are conditioned to trust. In the Staples and Dell campaigns, the suspicious content was a phone number placed into transactional fields. In list bombing and registration abuse, the lure can appear inside reflected account or profile data. In bounce abuse, the malicious content may sit inside returned message data or a nested MIME object. 

Defending against this requires content-aware validation at multiple points in the delivery chain. Platform owners should treat any user-controlled value rendered into an email template as untrusted data. Fields used for names, addresses, company names, project titles, order notes or support instructions should be validated before storage and again before rendering. Phone numbers, URLs, markup, line breaks, and urgent support language should be rejected or flagged when they appear in fields where they do not belong.  

Security gateways should inspect the fully rendered message, not only the sender or template. That includes HTML, text, URLs, redirects, attachments, personalization fields, and nested MIME content. For transactional email, defenders should also evaluate whether the message content aligns with the workflow that produced it. An order notification containing unexpected support numbers, cancellation instructions, or high-urgency language should be treated differently from a routine receipt. 

For delivery reports, recursive MIME inspection is especially important. Gateways should parse DSN containers, extract returned messages or message fragments, and apply normal phishing, malware, and URL analysis to the nested content. A bounce should explain a delivery failure, not provide a blind path for untrusted payloads. 

The broader lesson is that attackers are no longer only exploiting technical vulnerabilities in infrastructure. They are exploiting the assumptions built into business processes. When legitimate systems render attacker-influenced data into trusted notifications, the result can pass authentication checks and still deliver malicious intent.  

Defenders should therefore treat sender trust and content trust as separate but complementary signals. The wrapper can explain where a message came from. It cannot prove that the payload is safe. 

Acknowledgments 

Special thanks to Eric Peterson, Dev Shah, and Adam Katz for their professional guidance and input during the development of this research.

item.title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
item.description: The September Microsoft Patch Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? And what does the future look like?
item.dc:creator: Kri Dontje
item.content:encoded:
• Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model. 
  • Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited. 
  • We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines. 
  • With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains. 

The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? 

As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions: 

  • If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed? 
  • Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old? 
  • Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed? 
  • How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers? 
  • Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end? 

The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization. 

Where is it from? 

AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities. 

Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability.  

Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j (CVE-2021-44228) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan. 

Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process (MAPP) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced.  "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says.  

Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines. 

For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work. 

The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question.  

Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades.  

Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released.  

This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux. 

Will it stay this high? 

No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight.  

Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off. 

When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year.  

Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way.  

While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right? 

Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly. 

As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly.  

There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system.  

However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem.  

Are the numbers the real issue? 

The volume is certainly up.  

Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month. 

With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities.  

Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story. 

Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises. 

AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness. 

For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths?  

What do we do now? 

The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not.  

Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role.  

For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks. 

For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP.  Don't stop there.  

  • For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own. 
  • Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms. 
  • Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge. 
  • Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains. 

Dive deeper into this conversation with the latest TTP interview with Yves Younan and vulnerability researcher Bella Fusari.

For more numbers and advice for defenders: 

  • Don't swing at everything 
  • Threat Source Newsletter: Discovery ≠ Exploitation

item.title: The Q3 Vulnerability Pulse: Discovery ≠ Exploitation
item.description: Is the cybersecurity world really facing a "Bugmageddon?" Thor breaks down the latest CVE and KEV trends in the latest Threat Source newsletter.
item.dc:creator: Thorsten Rosendahl
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. 

I've been following a lot of (sometimes heated) threads and discussions lately about the current vulnerability landscape. I learned new words/phrases such as Summer of Hell (although I'm writing this with 1°C/34°F outside), Vulnpocalypse, Bugmageddon, Bugpocalypse, Breachpocalypse... 

Let's look at some numbers:

We crossed the 70k mark, and it's only the end of September. This has never been seen before — I think we can agree this number is skyrocketing. Also, CVE numbering organically grew into the six-digit range. Check your tooling. Some might say we broke that barrier already in 2014 (CVE-2014-125110), or even hit seven digits in 2015 (CVE-2015-1000013), but those were allocated artificially. (History note: Before 2014, 9999 was the highest possible identifier.) 

So that could be seen as the apocalypse argument. On the other hand, we have the KEV numbers:

They didn't explode... yet? Counting by sheer volume, YoY, CVEs increased by 105%, while KEV only grew 37%. Sounds huge at first, but following a 30% increase from 2024 to 2025, that's less dramatic — a counter-argument of sorts.

CVEs from 2025 or older still account for 33%. In other words, a good third of the KEVs are suggesting there is a patch gap. Looking at the 2026 CVEs, the share where the publication date matches the date added to KEV is 29%, which is only 2% more than (all of) 2025. Acknowledging this "math" is not the whole ball of wax, but it still tells me we are not living in a zero-day apocalypse right now. There’s also a slight uptick in networking gear-related CVEs, to 27%.

This is the second time I'll ask you to check your tooling. A new column, “forensicTriage,” was added to the KEV to flag which high-risk vulnerabilities require mandatory forensic triage and incident response workflows. You can read more about it in BOD 26-04, or the Implementation Guidance. 

So where does that leave us? The CVE numbers alone — that +70k mark, now that Q3 is behind us — make a decent case for Vulnpocalypse, or whichever name you prefer. That part of the story is real. But discovery isn't exploitation, and that gap is exactly what the KEV numbers remind us of. Vendors seem to be keeping pace too, at least partially — KEV is growing, just not nearly at CVE's speed, which on its own would almost be good news. 

Where the story breaks down is on the practical side. More than a third of actively exploited vulnerabilities still trace back to 2025 or earlier. Patch debt doesn't care how many new apocalypse-themed hashtags we invent. 

So, panic? I still don't think so. Relax? Definitely not either. Somewhere between the two is where the real work sits — chipping away at that backlog, one legacy system at a time. Maybe by next quarter it'll feel less like Bugmageddon and more like business as usual. Or maybe I won't even need a warmer jacket for the upcoming "Winter of Hell."

The one big thing  

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future’s Insikt Group are disclosing new espionage activity from UAT-6275 targeting government and critical infrastructure across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Thanks to the threat actor's own operational security lapses, researchers gained direct visibility into their infrastructure and malware development. We observed four distinct infection chains delivering custom reverse shells via macro-enabled documents, GitHub-hosted scripts, and a WinRAR vulnerability. 

Why do I care? 

Regional government and critical infrastructure entities are actively being targeted for diplomatic and economic intelligence. UAT-6275 is consistently evolving its tradecraft, abusing legitimate platforms like GitHub to host payloads and deploying lightweight reverse shells. Furthermore, recovered tooling suggests the group is preparing to expand its reach into Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances. 

So now what? 

Defenders in targeted regions and sectors should monitor for unexpected PowerShell activity and payload downloads originating from public services like GitHub. It is also critical to watch for suspicious scheduled tasks and unauthorized changes to the Windows Startup folder, which this group uses for persistence. Finally, ensure archive utilities are fully patched to prevent exploit-assisted delivery. ClamAV signatures and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to detect this threat can be found in the full blog post. 

Top security headlines of the week 

Hackers heat supermarket fridges to 50°C in France cyber attack 
The attack began overnight from Sunday to Monday. The unknown attackers reportedly abused the defrosting function in older control software, setting some equipment to heat continuously, with temperatures said to have reached 50°C. (Hack Read) 

Ivanti zero-day chain gave attackers root access to fully patched VPN 
CVE-2026-104935 affects Ivanti Connect Secure and it can be exploited for unauthenticated remote code execution with elevated privileges. (SecurityWeek) 

U.S. arrests two in crackdown on North Korean IT worker laptop farms
As part of the scheme, which allegedly ran between 2019 and July 2025, the two housed and configured laptops issued by victim U.S. companies so ITWs would appear to work from the U.S. (SecurityWeek) 

Canadian cybersecurity executive arrested in U.S. federal extortion case 
While the FBI did not publicly announce Dubrovsky’s arrest, the case appears to align with actions taken in the wake of the ShinyHunters’ attack on the FBI’s IT systems, which exposed personal data about thousands of bureau employees. (CyberScoop) 

Maximum-severity SSRF flaw in SonicWall SMA devices under attack 
The vulnerability, which SonicWall assigned a maximum 10 out of 10 CVSS score, stems from an "unintended alternate access path," according to the vendor's advisory. (Dark Reading) 

Can’t get enough Talos? 

You've got to lurk before you can smirk 
How do you get under a cybercriminal’s skin? Sometimes you expose their operations. Sometimes you make every step through a network painfully slow. And sometimes, if you’re Azim, you join a dark web forum where they’re insulting you, and help them to do it. 

Microsoft Patch Tuesday for October 2026 
Microsoft has released its monthly security update for October 2026, which includes 1,415 vulnerabilities affecting a range of products, including 85 that Microsoft marked as "critical." 

One breach, please, and make no mistakes 
The cybersecurity community has seen examples of autonomous agents, built inside AI labs, attacking public infrastructure. How you prepare for agentic threats is what makes the difference during real incidents.

item.title: Break the silence: Kazakhstan-nexus UAT-6275 targets CIS government organizations
item.description: Talos and Recorded Future identified UAT-6275 activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States. Recovered artifacts show additional interest in water resources and energy.
item.dc:creator: Ashley Shen
item.content:encoded:
This research was conducted jointly with Julian-Ferdinand Vögele of Recorded Future’s Insikt Group. Details of the joint research and presentation are available here.

  • Cisco Talos identified UAT-6275 (TAG-193 by Recorded Future) activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Recovered artifacts show additional interest in water resources and energy. This focus is consistent with intelligence collection and may reflect the regional effects of the Russia–Ukraine war. 
  • In activity observed from June 2025 through August 2026, Talos identified four infection-chain types that use macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and a crafted WinRAR archive exploiting CVE-2025-8088. The recovered payloads include several custom reverse shells that provide interactive remote access. 
  • Three publicly accessible staging directories and GitHub repository history exposed payload builds, tool inventories, and changes to command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. These operational security lapses gave us direct visibility into the group's recent activity. 
  • The files recovered from the exposed infrastructure suggest preparation for post-compromise operations and potential activity against Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.  
  • Talos assesses with medium confidence that UAT-6275 has a Kazakhstan nexus, based on infrastructure access, language artifacts, sample submissions, working hours analysis, and regional targeting interests.

Background 

Cisco Talos and Recorded Future Insikt Group jointly investigated UAT-6275 activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The investigation uncovered three publicly accessible staging directories and a previously unreported GitHub repository used to host malicious scripts and payloads. These exposed assets provided visibility into the threat actor's malware development, infrastructure changes and preparations for additional intrusion activity. 

Talos tracks this activity as UAT-6275, while Recorded Future tracks it as TAG-193. It overlaps with Silent Lynx (first reported by Seqrite) and sits within a broader set of campaigns connected to YoroTrooper, which we first reported in 2023. Subsequent research on Tomiris (Kaspersky), ShadowSilk (Group-IB), Cavalry Werewolf (BI.ZONE), and Hydra Saiga (VMRay) identified overlapping indicators across these reported clusters. We assess that UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper likely belong to the same broader activity cluster. However, we continue to track them separately because we have not observed direct indicator or toolset overlap between the two.

This post summarizes our joint Virus Bulletin 2026 white paper, “Break the silence: tracking Silent Lynx through exposed infrastructure” which contains the full technical analysis and indicators of compromise (IOCs).

Victimology 

UAT-6275's targeting is concentrated in Central Asia and the wider CIS region. Across the reviewed campaigns, observed victims and lure themes span nine countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus.

Government and diplomatic affairs 

UAT-6275 targets government institutions responsible for diplomacy, economic development, agriculture, and environmental management. These organizations hold information that can inform bilateral negotiations, economic planning, and regional security decisions.

Our network flow analysis identified activity involving a Tajik government entity shortly after treaty discussions with Kazakhstan in March 2026 and a Belarusian government entity ahead of a bilateral meeting in April. This timing may indicate an interest in regional diplomatic developments.

The decoy documents we recovered also suggest an interest in diplomatic relations, international trade, and aviation. Examples include a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Water security and resource management 

The group’s interest in regional resources spans environmental management and energy. Talos observed activity involving an Armenian government entity responsible for environmental matters and Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative, consistent with earlier reporting on Silent Lynx targeting water resource organizations across Central Asia. 

Energy-themed decoys included a cooperation proposal between Turkmenistan’s state oil company, Turkmennebit, and Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery, used in an August 2025 sample. The refinery supplies petroleum products to Kazakhstan and later shut down after a Ukrainian drone strike in August 2026, with repairs expected to take up to six months. These ties suggest a possible intelligence interest in regional fuel supplies and the war’s implications for Kazakhstan’s energy security.

Campaign timeline 

Since Seqrite first reported Silent Lynx in January 2025, we have identified at least eight campaigns across the region through May 2026. These include malware delivery targeting Russia, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan; a credential-harvesting site impersonating Azerbaijan’s State Agency for Public Service; and lures referencing the China–Central Asia Summit and Russian energy infrastructure. In 2026, we also observed activity involving government entities in Tajikistan, Armenia, and Belarus, as well as Uzbekistan’s Smart Forestry initiative in May. 

Infrastructure and malware delivery 

Talos identified three publicly accessible staging directories containing malware and tools of UAT-6275. One sample led to the previously unreported GitHub repository, where the group hosted PowerShell scripts and payloads. Its commit history allowed us to track infrastructure changes and malware development.

The group relies on lightweight reverse shells, including Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell, to issue commands on compromised systems.

We also recovered Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for FortiWeb CVE-2025-25257 from UAT-6275 infrastructure. These findings suggest interest in expanding the group’s operational capabilities. 

Four infection chains 

UAT-6275 used malicious documents, executable downloaders, and shortcuts to deliver malware, and later incorporated a WinRAR exploit. Talos categorized the recovered samples into four infection chains, A – D, based on how they retrieve and execute their payloads.

The first Chain A samples, observed in June 2025, used macro-enabled Word documents to download and execute a second-stage binary. In July 2025, we observed Chain B downloaders built with PS2EXE, a tool that packages PowerShell scripts as standalone Windows executables. These downloaders retrieved reverse-shell payloads and created scheduled tasks for persistence. 

We first observed Chain C in October 2025. A malicious shortcut launches PowerShell to retrieve and execute a GitHub-hosted script that provides remote shell access. Later samples also downloaded PickleShell and placed it in the Windows Startup folder for persistence.

In April 2026, we identified a RAR archive that exploited CVE-2025-8088 in WinRAR to place PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder (Chain D). The payload runs at the next user sign-in. This was the first vulnerability exploit we observed in UAT-6275’s malware delivery.

Kazakhstan nexus assessment 

Talos assesses with medium confidence that UAT-6275 has a Kazakhstan nexus. Supporting evidence includes Russian-language artifacts, apparent malware-testing submissions from Kazakhstan shortly after compilation, and operator activity consistent with UTC+5 working hours.

Looking ahead 

UAT-6275’s sustained activity and adoption of new delivery techniques suggest the group will continue pursuing access to government organizations across Central Asia and the CIS. Its interest in environmental agencies, economic ministries, and energy infrastructure reflects the intelligence value of regional diplomacy and resource management. 

Defenders in these sectors should monitor unexpected PowerShell activity and payload downloads from public services such as GitHub, alongside scheduled tasks and Startup-folder changes. Keeping archive utilities patched can help reduce exposure to the exploit-assisted delivery observed in this campaign. 

For further details on this research and our accompanying presentation, see “Break the Silence: Tracking Silent Lynx Through Exposed Infrastructure” on Virus Bulletin’s website, as well as Recorded Future’s related blog post.

Coverage 

The following ClamAV signatures detect and block this threat: 

  • Win.Backdoor.PickleShell-10060602-0 
  • Win.Backdoor.Chvost-10060603-0 
  • Win.Malware.Generic-10060604-0 
  • Win.Malware.LAPLAS-10060605-0 
  • Win.Malware.LAPLAS-10060606-0 
  • Win.Proxy.Generic-10060628-0 

The following Snort rules cover this threat: 

  • Snort 2: 1:11192, 1:15306, 1:46983, 1:47398 
  • Snort 3: 1:46983, 4:16 

IOCs

IOCs for this research can be found at our GitHub repository here.

item.content:encoded:
Microsoft has released its monthly security update for October 2026, which includes 1415 vulnerabilities affecting a range of products, including 85 that Microsoft marked as "critical."

Microsoft notes that 1 of the vulnerabilities disclosed this month have been exploited in the wild

CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass vulnerability that affects Windows Shell. The shared weakness is Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in a Command ('Command Injection'). The vulnerability has a CVSS base score of 8.8.

Out of 85 "critical" vulnerabilities, 67 are remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.

item.title: Making sure the checks get printed
item.description: Pierre's debut newsletter explores the messy, real-world side of risk management and how to keep vital systems running when a perfect patch isn't an option.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Cadieux
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. 

My name is Pierre Cadieux, and I’ll be helping contribute to these newsletters. A little about me: I’ve been working in the cybersecurity industry in many roles over the past 20+ years, first focusing on endpoint security, policies, and firewalls, then moving to risk management and compliance, disaster recovery, and investigations. I spent about 15 years as a consultant working across many well-known consultancy firms and eventually moved to Cisco where I spent time doing security operations center (SOC) design and assessments as well as segmentation before moving to the Talos IR team. I spent many years there, first as an Incident Commander and then a manager of our excellent team of global IR consultants and investigators. My current role is with the Talos Threat Intelligence and Interdiction team, where I’m focused on intelligence efficacy — how we can do better with the data we have, how we can get more data, and what our customers want from our intelligence products. 

Since it’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month, I wanted to take a few minutes to collectively thank all of the defenders out there for the hard work you do each day. The work you do may not always be visible, but it matters.  

I remember one job I had many years ago when I was in charge of security for a financial institution. I spent time learning each of the business processes that we had so I could understand each of the moving parts, what was essential, and what was on the horizon for change. I even spent a couple days meeting with the folks who handled printing. Yeah, printing — but not reports or internal documents. These were the people that created the checks that our institution used to pay other institutions, and more importantly (to me) our customers. 

I recall there being many out-of-patch compliance boxes in this area of the company, so I, being the diligent Director, decided to find out why. It turns out the software being used to print these business essential checks would not run on the current operating systems, and the physical printer cards used to connect to these non-network printers also required older hardware ports. As one of the people I interviewed said, “We don’t want to be the reason someone’s grandma doesn’t get her check and can’t go to the grocery store.” 

There were (at the time) no other alternatives that we could deploy, and the environment had zero tolerance for downtime. The solution I proposed was to isolate these devices into their own network, which blocked access to and from the internet for these devices, and also reduced the likelihood that these devices would be identified during an adversary’s internal reconnaissance or mapping. It didn’t patch the vulnerable devices, but it went a long way to reducing the likelihood of a bad thing happening to these devices due to their out-of-date OS and software. 

This story is especially appropriate today, as we face ever-increasing numbers of vulnerabilities announced by software vendors, and can only expect this volume to continue to increase. Do what you can to make sure the checks still get printed, while managing your risks intentionally. 

The one big thing  

Cisco Talos is disclosing new findings from our CAIRN research that show malware authors are embedding natural-language instructions into their code to evade AI-assisted analysis. We classify this growing trend as "A3: AI-Analysis Evasion." Over the past 18 months, we've tracked techniques ranging from simple comments telling an AI to ignore a file, to advanced "template spraying" designed to trick specific large language models (LLMs).  

Why do I care? 

Attackers expect AI to be in your analysis pipeline, and they’re developing cheap methods to manipulate those systems. While we found these prompt-injection techniques only steer the AI's verdict in the attacker's favor about 35 percent of the time, they are being adopted across all levels of malware sophistication. A3 families like MANTLEMAZE also pair these AI deceptions with serious underlying threats, such as abusing vulnerable drivers to disable EDR from kernel space. 

So now what? 

Because these evasion instructions must be written in plaintext, defenders have a highly stable detection surface to monitor. Security teams should flag imperative language addressed to analysis systems within binaries as a suspicious signal. Most importantly, anyone building or using AI-assisted pipelines must ensure that text extracted from a sample is strictly treated as evidence, never as a system directive. Read the full blog for more information on these techniques and a list of sample hashes. 

Top security headlines of the week 

Citrix NetScaler security snafus get even worse amid more zero-day reports 
This latest vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-88779, is a memory overflow bug that leads to denial of service attacks. (The Register) 

Hackers steal 8 million citizens’ records from Danish government database 
The Danish government would not say who is behind the breach, which happened in September but was discovered on October 2. However, it said the unauthorized access was obtained by “abusing a Danish company’s lawful access to search for information in the CPR system.” (TechCrunch) 

Google narrows open-source bug bounty amid wave of invalid automated reports 
Google has temporarily closed its Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program (OSS VRP) to product vulnerability submissions. According to Google, it has no impact on the program’s supply chain reports or on any pending reports. (SecurityWeek) 

Warlock ransomware hits large Spanish, Portuguese orgs 
In the last two months, researchers observed Warlock attacks against four victims: a water utility, a telecommunications provider, a regional government body, and a university. (Dark Reading) 

U.S. Senate passes health care cybersecurity bill after 190 million impacted by Change Healthcare breach 
The Health Care Cybersecurity and Resiliency Act of 2026 was passed by unanimous consent last week, potentially expanding federal cyber requirements for health care organizations. (The Record) 

Can’t get enough Talos? 

One breach, please, and make no mistakes 
The cybersecurity community has seen examples of autonomous agents, built inside AI labs, attacking public infrastructure. How you prepare for agentic threats is what makes the difference during real incidents. 

Talos Takes: Honey, I Trapped the Adversary 
It’s time to start having fun and messing with your attackers. For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, Martin Lee joins Amy to discuss the fine art of making life on your network a complete nightmare for adversaries. 

The Fine Art of Frustrating the Adversary 
What really frustrates an adversary? Eight Cisco Talos researchers share practical ways to make their next move slower and riskier, from deception and behavioral detection to breaking attack dependencies.

item.title: UAT-11985: AI-assisted event lures delivering real-time Google AitM phishing
item.description: Cisco Talos identified an APT spear-phishing campaign against individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations. The operation leveraged legitimate public event themes and impersonated reputable academic and policy institutions.
item.dc:creator: Joey Chen
item.content:encoded:
• Cisco Talos identified an advanced persistent threat (APT) spear-phishing campaign against individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations. The operation leveraged legitimate public event themes and impersonated reputable academic and policy institutions to establish credibility. 
  • The phishing emails exhibited highly consistent structure, rhetoric, and personalization patterns, suggesting the threat actor likely used AI-assisted content generation to rapidly customize invitation lures for different targets while maintaining a common social engineering framework. 
  • Beyond traditional email phishing, the actor incorporated QR code phishing (quishing) techniques by modifying legitimate event posters with malicious QR codes, expanding the attack surface beyond email recipients to secondary victims who may encounter printed materials. 
  • The campaign deployed an advanced adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing framework that impersonated Google authentication pages and utilized a hybrid HTTP and WebSocket architecture to synchronize authentication workflows in real time, enabling the interception of credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) challenges. 
  • After technical analysis of the phishing kit, Talos assesses with moderate confidence that the user interface was originally developed in Simplified Chinese and later adapted for Traditional Chinese and English. The localization architecture, Simplified Chinese default language branch, and mainland-Chinese lexical usage collectively suggest a developer whose primary working language is Simplified Chinese.

In mid-2026, Talos observed an APT spear-phishing campaign targeting Taiwan-based research organizations. The threat actor appeared to reuse legitimate or plausible public event information, then embedded a hyperlink to actor-controlled infrastructure, while the displayed URL appeared benign. Several invitation emails exhibited nearly identical syntactic structures despite discussing different geopolitical topics, suggesting the content was generated from a reusable prompt template rather than independently authored. While Talos cannot conclusively determine whether the emails were fully generated by a large language model (LLM), the campaign demonstrates strong evidence of AI-assisted content production and personalization. 

Spear-phishing mail 

Based on the phishing emails we observed, the threat actor impersonated legitimate institutions in Taiwan such as Taiwan European Union Centre, NCCU Institute of International Relations, and Taiwan Research Institute. Below is a deep analysis of the mail contents.

An email recipient contacted the organizations concerned to verify the purported senders. However, none of the organizations could confirm that the three senders were employees or representatives of the institutions named in the emails. This suggests that the threat actor fabricated the sender identities while using legitimate organizational names and publicly available event information as cover.

All three emails follow a highly consistent, three-part structure, indicating the use of a common template. The opening section provides a polished (but overly elaborate) description of the geopolitical or policy context. It relies heavily on grandiose yet vague expressions such as “the global strategic landscape,” “reshaping the great-power order,” “three-dimensional analysis,” “forward looking and in-depth analysis,” and “high intensity professional dialogue” to create an impression of academic authority and subject matter expertise. Although the language is generally fluent, the excessive use of policy jargon and abstract strategic terminology makes the content appear formulaic.

The second section is customized for the recipient and uses targeted flattery to encourage engagement. Similar phrases including “admiration,” “authoritative perspective,” “highly perceptive,” and “key practical dimensions” appear across the three messages. These compliments are broadly applicable and contain few verifiable details about the recipient’s actual work, suggesting that the actor personalized a reusable template using publicly available professional information. References to exclusive participation, reserved VIP seating, or the recipient’s supposedly unique expertise further exploit professional recognition and status to reduce suspicion.

The final section presents event logistics, including the topic, date, venue, and registration instructions. Although much of this information appears to have been copied from legitimate institutional websites or public event announcements, its accuracy does not validate the email or the sender. Instead, the actor appears to use authentic event details as a form of legitimacy laundering. The registration links embedded in the emails do not direct recipients to the legitimate event registration pages they seem to represent. For example, one hyperlink displays a legitimate-looking Google Forms URL, while its underlying href redirects the recipient to a deceptive phishing site hosted on a third-party platform. This mismatch between the visible link text and the actual destination demonstrates a deliberate attempt to conceal the phishing infrastructure and exploit the recipient’s trust in a familiar service.

Taken together, the reuse of an almost-identical narrative structure, rhetorical style, personalized flattery, institutional impersonation, and deceptive registration mechanism strongly suggests a coordinated and carefully targeted spear-phishing campaign rather than three independent invitations. The messages also exhibit characteristics consistent with AI-assisted content generation such as grammatically fluent but formulaic prose, excessive use of grandiose and abstract policy terminology, interchangeable praise, repetitive sentence patterns, and rapid customization for different recipients, institutions, and geopolitical topics. Although these linguistic indicators alone cannot conclusively prove the use of generative AI, their consistency across all three emails suggests that the threat actor likely used an AI-assisted template to produce and personalize the phishing lures at scale. The legitimate event details and visible Google Forms URLs were then combined with disguised hyperlinks leading to actor-controlled phishing pages, making the emails appear credible while concealing their actual destination. 

Quishing in the poster 

We also observed the threat actor attaching event posters to several phishing emails. While the poster designs were scraped from legitimate websites, the embedded QR codes were maliciously altered. This modification indicates a calculated physical world attack vector. The actor may have anticipated that recipients might print and display these posters on office bulletin boards, thereby tricking other individuals into scanning the malicious QR code to register for the event. By doing so, the threat actor expands their attack vector beyond traditional email phishing to include quishing (QR code phishing), and broadens their reach within the targeted entities.

Phishing kit used by UAT-11985 

Phishing page’s impersonation 

These three phishing email attacks use the same tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) which include a phishing page impersonating a legitimate Google Form and appearing visually identical to the authentic service. However, aligned with the threat actor's primary objective of credential theft, the malicious form forcibly redirects the user to a spoofed Google login page.

Talos observed that the spoofed Google login panels only support Simplified Chinese (zh-CN), Traditional Chinese (zh-TW), and English locales, with region detection based on the victim's browser “navigator.languages”, strongly suggesting targeting of Chinese-speaking users.

We also observed that this phishing page revealed a hidden HTML <section> designed to simulate a successful Google authentication event. Within this structure, the threat actor embedded an iframe (ID: google-success-frame) configured to load a locally hosted asset (/google-login-assets/operation-success.html). Notably, the iframe includes the sandbox="allow-scripts" attribute. We will discuss JavaScript in the next section.

Attack summary  

The attack chain initiates when a victim clicks a malicious URL delivered via a phishing email. Upon access, the victim is presented with a pixel-perfect replica of the Google sign-in page, which covertly hosts an obfuscated JavaScript payload. Operating as an adversary in the middle (AitM), the threat actor positions their infrastructure between the victim's browser and legitimate Google authentication servers. This allows them to seamlessly forward credentials and dynamically control the victim's user interface step-by-step via a persistent WebSocket connection.

To evade detection and complicate analysis, the malicious JavaScript is embedded at the end of the HTML document and relies on advanced string rotation obfuscation. The script leverages a large, static array of Base64 encoded strings coupled with control flow obfuscation. By utilizing a while(!![]) { push/shift } shuffle loop mechanism, the array rotation is resolved dynamically at runtime, effectively thwarting automated static deobfuscation tools.

Talos’ analysis of the phishing kit's client-side JavaScript indicates, with moderate confidence, that the user interface localization was authored by a native Simplified Chinese speaker. The strongest indicator is the kit's localization architecture:  

  1. The base translation object (T) is written entirely in Simplified Chinese and is directly assigned as the zh-CN locale, while the Traditional Chinese (zh-TW) and English (en) locales are derived from it at runtime via an override or merge function (v(T, {...})).  
  2. This structure demonstrates that the interface was originally composed in Simplified Chinese and subsequently translated into Traditional Chinese and English, consistent with Simplified Chinese being the developer's primary working language.
  3. This assessment is reinforced by lexical choices characteristic of mainland Chinese usage rather than Taiwanese, Hong Kong, or Southeast Asian conventions. For example, the text uses Simplified Chinese forms such as “账号” for “account,” whereas Traditional Chinese environments would more commonly use “帳號” or related variants. Similarly, terms such as “计算机” for “computer,” “邮箱” for “email/mailbox,” “无痕浏览窗口” for “incognito browsing window,” and “访客模式” for “guest mode” reflect terminology commonly seen in mainland-oriented Simplified Chinese software localization. In Taiwanese or Hong Kong contexts, these concepts are typically rendered with Traditional Chinese characters and often different localized wording, such as “電腦,” “電子郵件/信箱,” or “無痕式視窗.” This linguistic pattern is further supported by the ternary-fallback ordering throughout the code, which consistently places Simplified Chinese as the default branch.

Operator-driven phishing page 

Following the deobfuscation and analysis of these JavaScript payloads, Talos identified an advanced, real-time AitM phishing kit targeting Google accounts. Unlike fully automated phishing kits, this framework appears optimized for operator-driven authentication orchestration. This kit impersonates the Google sign-in interface across three locales (zh-CN, zh-TW, en) and employs a dual-channel architecture including HTTP POST and WebSocket to synchronize Google's authentication state in real time. This mechanism effectively bypasses multi-factor authentication (MFA) to harvest complete, authenticated session tokens.

The threat actor deliberately employs a split communication channel architecture to optimize both data exfiltration and real-time command and control (C2) efficiency. For the outbound data exfiltration, the threat actor utilized HTTP POST for stateless, event-driven data transmission. The phishing page actively pushes captured data to the C2 server, including initial browser fingerprints, credential and challenge submissions during user interaction, and periodic heartbeat polls to maintain synchronization. Each call completes independently.

The threat actor uses WebSocket to provide a low-latency, persistent connection. The C2 server streams real-time instructions to the phishing page via this channel, dictating exactly which MFA challenge screen to render. Cisco Talos has also recently published a report on a different phishing campaign where similar WebSocket techniques were observed in a phishing kit used by a Chinese-speaking actor. However, the strategies employed by that phishing kit differ from those in this case.

The following diagram illustrates the real-time AitM relay architecture.

At the beginning phase, the threat actor collects device and browser information, including the locale, user agent, screen dimensions, and mobile-device status. This data is sent to the actor’s HTTP C2 server through a google_login_start request. After the server creates a session, the JavaScript establishes a WebSocket connection with the actor’s C2 infrastructure and receives a snapshot containing the current session state.

The victim enters an email address or phone number into the fake Google login page. The phishing page sends the identifier to the actor’s HTTP C2 server using the google_input_identifier event. The actor’s server then relays the identifier to the real Google authentication service to verify whether the account exists and determines whether a passkey-based flow is enabled. Based on Google’s response, the actor instructs the phishing page through WebSocket state updates to display either the password-entry page or a passkey prompt.

When the victim submits a password, the phishing page sends the password, account identifier, and browser user-agent information to the actor’s HTTP C2 server through a google_login_check request. The actor’s server forwards the credentials to the real Google authentication service. If the credentials are accepted and Google requires additional authentication, the server returns the MFA challenge type and layout. The actor then advances the victim’s interface to the appropriate MFA step through a WebSocket update.

By deliberately splitting one-shot uploads with POST requests from low-latency state updates with WebSocket connection, the threat actor has engineered a seamless credential-harvesting relay. This allows the threat actor to mirror Google's dynamic authentication state in real time, ultimately achieving full account takeover without raising the victim's suspicion.

Coverage  

The following ClamAV signatures detect and block this threat:  

  • Html.Phishing.UAT11985-10060614-0 

The following SNORT® rules (SIDs) detect and block this threat:   

  • Snort2: 1:67198
  • Snort3: 7:31
